blocks.text: …being out and about in calm
Definition and purpose 🐕
Stress tolerance is the ability of the dog handler to act emotionally independently of the respective situation.
Stress tolerance is the ability of the dog not to react immediately out of drive under strong stimulation – and to be able to rely on trained sequences.

Stress tolerance is the ability of the dog handler to convey calm and trust to the dog under pressure – and the ability of the dog to trust the handler in stimulating situations and to remain responsive to leadership.

Note: Stress tolerance training in the city is primarily training for us dog owners. As a team player, our dog depends to a good extent on our behaviour. The way we conduct ourselves is how our dog will express it outwardly.
Prerequisite: Preventive training of the TEAM WALK is very helpful for implementing stress tolerance training in urban areas.

The route 🚶
We walk in a balanced way at a relaxed walking pace and train ourselves to take adverse circumstances calmly.
We perceive our surroundings attentively and promptly realise what is happening around us.
We react quickly as needed and otherwise embody composure.
We set an example of relaxed self-confidence for our dog and open up positive options for action to it in every situation.
Options for action and de-escalation 📋
As soon as a situation threatens to turn into a stressful one, we collect ourselves mentally and briefly direct our perception to grasping the overall situation and recognising our options.
Options for action: Moving aside – Turning back – Holding still – Continuing on
De-escalation options: Giving space – Turning away – Distracting – Calming – Engaging
The principle is: MOVE ASIDE, TURN AWAY and ENGAGE POSITIVELY.
Case 1 – Moving aside 🔀
If we can see that there is a way to step out of the developing situation to the side (open area, paths, driveways, grass verges, etc.), this is the first choice.

We walk briskly but not hectically – more as if it had been our intention anyway – out of the situation until our dog follows us reasonably again. We leave with the leash held at its normal length. It should on no account be shortened too quickly, as this would sharply increase the dog’s excitement.

If we sense that it is calming down, we may stop and calmly bring our dog into “down” or, in more difficult conditions, into “sit”. The dog’s line of sight during the exercise should be turned away from the source of the stimulus as far as possible.
After the situation has completely subsided, we praise our dog extensively once the command has been released.
ATTENTION: Never praise too early – on no account while the situation or the arousal phase is still going on. Always praise only after a calm, secured situation has been established.
Case 2 – Turning back 🔁
If there is NO possibility of moving aside far enough to the side, a purposeful turning back and leaving of the situation is to be chosen.

We turn briskly but not hectically – more as if it had been our intention anyway – in a loose arc without hesitating, and walk back without interruption until an opportunity to move aside to the side arises.

Turning back is done with the leash held at its normal length. Frequent restless behaviour of the dog towards the distraction is normal and we do not comment on it further, as this would contribute to an unwanted confirmation of the behaviour.
As soon as the dog signals readiness by following relatively willingly, moving aside to the side follows – from then on proceed as under Case 1 .

ATTENTION: Never stand still for long and think it over! In case of doubt and confrontation, always turn back and walk away instinctively and with little emotion. Simply take the dog along on a leash held at normal length and later look for a quiet spot to the side at a safe distance.
Case 3 – Holding still ⏸️

If we are suddenly and unavoidably surprised by a stressful situation and there is neither room to move aside nor time to turn back, one thing above all remains for us: calm, calm and once again calm.
If our dog, happily, stays calm, we do nothing further and let the situation pass.
Otherwise, we turn away from the situation smoothly together with the dog. We simply turn away and take our dog around with us on a more shortly held leash.
ATTENTION: Never grab the collar or harness. The dog interprets this strong restriction as an additional problem and may therefore react violently.
Once we have turned away as well as possible, we control the dog on a short leash and gradually bring it calmly into “sit” – without developing stress. Speed is not what matters, only calm composure.
After the situation has been overcome, we bring our dog into “down” and let the situation fade out in peace as a learning experience. We finish with “sit” and extensive, trusting praise.
Case 4 – Continuing on ▶️

In extremely overstimulated, unpredictable encounter situations, it can be very advisable not to make the overall situation worse by training measures that cannot be implemented – and instead to clear the area quickly.

To do this, the dog is led briskly through the situation without losing time and without interrupting the walking rhythm, by the shortest possible route and at the greatest possible distance from the source of the stimulus, on a leash held, if possible, not too short.
The rule here: Talk as little as possible, walk as confidently as necessary – until we have clearly left the stimulus area.
There we put our dog into “down” as a positive conclusion and let the situation fade until it is relaxed.
Important notes ⚠️
Avoid holding the dog by the collar or harness – in stressful situations this provokes the dog into self-defence and thus into escalation.
Avoid talking at the dog excessively or making loud remarks to third parties – the dog interprets this as a state of alarm.
Avoid hesitant behaviour – the dog will then necessarily take the initiative.
Avoid giving in to the situation – stay focused on your dog and on calmly working through the training sequences.
Avoid agitation and never adopt the stress level of the situation – stay calm and composed.
Practical impulse: First collect yourself, then act

The next time you find yourself in a stressful situation: take one short breath before you act. This one moment of collecting yourself decides whether you lead with calm or with reaction. Your dog is waiting for your signal – give it the right one.
